scenes.visual: Title card: TWO HINGES PER RESIDUE.

scenes.tts: A chain of a hundred residues looks as if it could bend any way at all. Can it?
scenes.visual: A long bead chain flops around freely on screen. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: A chain of a hundred residues looks as if it could bend any way at all. Can it?

scenes.tts: The answer starts with the bond that joins one residue to the next. It is the peptide bond.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the link between two beads. Label: peptide bond.
scenes.narration: The answer starts with the bond that joins one residue to the next. It is the peptide bond.

scenes.tts: It joins the carbon of one residue's C O group to the nitrogen of the next residue's N H group.
scenes.caption: It joins the carbon of one residue's C=O group to the nitrogen of the next residue's N–H group.
scenes.visual: Schematic atom letters appear at the link: C with an O above it, N with an H below it. The C–N link is highlighted.
scenes.narration: It joins the carbon of one residue's C=O group to the nitrogen of the next residue's N–H group.

scenes.tts: Chemists can draw this bond two ways.
scenes.visual: Two side-by-side panels appear, labelled form 1 and form 2.
scenes.narration: Chemists can draw this bond two ways.

scenes.tts: In one drawing, carbon and oxygen share a double bond. The bond from carbon to nitrogen is single.
scenes.visual: Form 1: C=O drawn as a double line, C–N as a single line.
scenes.narration: In one drawing, carbon and oxygen share a double bond. The bond from carbon to nitrogen is single.

scenes.tts: In the other, oxygen carries a negative charge. Carbon and nitrogen share a double bond, and nitrogen carries a positive charge.
scenes.visual: Form 2: C–O⁻ with a single line and a minus sign; C=N⁺ with a double line and a plus sign.
scenes.narration: In the other, oxygen carries a negative charge. Carbon and nitrogen share a double bond, and nitrogen carries a positive charge.

scenes.tts: The real bond is a blend of both. So the bond from carbon to nitrogen is partly double.
scenes.visual: The two panels slide together and fade into one drawing; the C–N line becomes one and a half lines thick. Label: partial double-bond character.
scenes.narration: The real bond is a blend of both. So the bond from carbon to nitrogen is partly double.

scenes.tts: That makes it short, about one point three two angstroms.
scenes.caption: That makes it short, about 1.32 Å.
scenes.visual: A small ruler under the C–N bond reads about 1.32 Å.
scenes.narration: That makes it short, about 1.32 Å.

scenes.tts: A double bond cannot twist without losing its overlap. So the peptide bond does not rotate.
scenes.visual: A curved arrow tries to twist the C–N bond and bounces back. A lock icon appears.
scenes.narration: A double bond cannot twist without losing its overlap. So the peptide bond does not rotate.

scenes.tts: Six atoms are locked in one flat plane.
scenes.visual: A translucent flat rectangle appears behind the bond, with six atom letters on it.
scenes.narration: Six atoms are locked in one flat plane.

scenes.tts: The alpha carbon of the first residue. Its carbon and oxygen. The nitrogen and hydrogen of the next residue. And that residue's alpha carbon.
scenes.caption: The Cα of the first residue. Its C and O. The N and H of the next residue. And that residue's Cα.
scenes.visual: Each atom lights up in turn as named: Cα, C, O, N, H, Cα.
scenes.narration: The Cα of the first residue. Its C and O. The N and H of the next residue. And that residue's Cα.

scenes.tts: Almost always, the two alpha carbons sit on opposite sides of the bond. That is the trans form.
scenes.visual: The two Cα atoms glow at opposite corners of the plane. Label: trans.
scenes.narration: Almost always, the two alpha carbons sit on opposite sides of the bond. That is the trans form.

scenes.tts: The cis form, with both on the same side, is rare. It is more common when the next residue is proline.
scenes.visual: A small inset: both Cα atoms on the same side, labelled cis, rare. A tag: more common at X–Pro bonds.
scenes.narration: The cis form, with both on the same side, is rare. It is more common when the next residue is proline.

scenes.tts: So picture the backbone as a string of flat, rigid cards. One card for each peptide bond.
scenes.visual: The plane becomes a flat card. More cards appear, linked corner to corner into a chain.
scenes.narration: So picture the backbone as a string of flat, rigid cards. One card for each peptide bond.

scenes.tts: The cards are joined at each alpha carbon. Watch what can move.
scenes.caption: The cards are joined at each Cα. Watch what can move.
scenes.visual: Each joint between cards is marked with a small dot labelled Cα.
scenes.narration: The cards are joined at each Cα. Watch what can move.

scenes.tts: Each residue has three backbone bonds. The peptide bond is frozen. Only two can turn, one on each side of the alpha carbon.
scenes.caption: Each residue has three backbone bonds. The peptide bond is frozen. Only two can turn, one on each side of the Cα.
scenes.visual: Three bonds per residue are labelled; the peptide bond shows a lock, the two bonds at the Cα joint show curved arrows.
scenes.narration: Each residue has three backbone bonds. The peptide bond is frozen. Only two can turn, one on each side of the Cα.

scenes.tts: Watch one hinge turn. It is the rotation about the bond from nitrogen to the alpha carbon. It is called fie.
scenes.caption: Watch one hinge turn. It is the rotation about the bond from nitrogen to the Cα. It is called phi.
scenes.visual: One card swings about the N–Cα bond. Once it has turned, the label appears: phi (φ), N–Cα.
scenes.narration: Watch one hinge turn. It is the rotation about the bond from nitrogen to the Cα. It is called phi.

scenes.tts: Now the other. It is the rotation about the bond from the alpha carbon to the next carbon. It is called sigh.
scenes.caption: Now the other. It is the rotation about the bond from the Cα to the next carbon. It is called psi.
scenes.visual: The next card swings about the Cα–C bond. Then the label appears: psi (ψ), Cα–C.
scenes.narration: Now the other. It is the rotation about the bond from the Cα to the next carbon. It is called psi.

scenes.tts: Two angles per residue, repeated down the chain. Together they set the path of the whole backbone.
scenes.visual: Every joint along the chain shows a φ and a ψ dial; the chain bends as the dials turn.
scenes.narration: Two angles per residue, repeated down the chain. Together they set the path of the whole backbone.

scenes.tts: Two free angles sound like freedom. Next, we see how much freedom they really give.
scenes.visual: The dials spin freely; a question mark appears over the chain.
scenes.narration: Two free angles sound like freedom. Next, we see how much freedom they really give.

scenes.tts: The peptide bond is flat and rigid. Each residue turns on just two hinges.
scenes.visual: End card. LINE: The peptide bond is flat and cannot twist, so each residue turns on just two hinges, phi and psi.
scenes.narration: The peptide bond is flat and rigid. Each residue turns on just two hinges.
